title: What is an ESG Fund? Your 2022 Guide
summary: Diginex is a pioneering sustainability reporting technology company and advisory firm dedicated to helping organizations navigate the complexities of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) compliance and Supply chain Analysis. |
body_text: ‍ The amount of money flowing into socially responsible investing is growing at a very rapid rate. By the close of 2018, the total ESG investments stood at USD30.7 trillion. This figure is expected to shoot up further and reach USD50 trillion in the next 20 years. ESG investing funds are strong vehicles that help to target bonds and equities based on how the issuing firms work towards promoting sustainability. So, how well do you know ESG funds investing? Keep reading as we dig deeper to answer pertinent questions, including, “ what is an ESG fund ?” and “what are the best tips for selecting the right funds?” ‍ ‍ What is an ESG Fund? ESG funds are bonds and equity portfolios that prioritize ESG factors in the investment methodologies. They pick on the securities that come with high sustainability scores while excluding those with rampant ESG issues, such as poor records on pollution and labor relations. Investors use ESG sustainability reports from the featured companies as part of doing due diligence on the companies of interest. High ESG scores mean that the companies are not just focused on optimizing profits but also committed to helping the planet become a better place for all. What You Need to Know about ESG Sustainability ESG, shortening for environmental, social and governance, is a set of criteria that help gauge an organization’s commitment to helping the globe address challenges facing it. They ensure that the organizations are responsible in their operations to reduce negative impacts on the environment, use ethical leadership, and uphold fairness/ integrity in governance. Here is a closer look at the three pillars of ESG and their application in investment funds: Environmental: This is the first ESG pillar and it targets to help investors identify investments that aim at improving the planet. Some of the core areas of focus are minimizing carbon footprint and cutting down wastes. Social: This pillar assesses how companies manage relationships with staff, partners, and communities. For example, are the employees in the targeted organizations remunerated well? Other social considerations might include supporting courses for social justice and improving the well-being of the community. Governance: Organizations that put focus on ESG value always prioritize the shareholders. Therefore, they always use transparent processes and offer updates that shareholders can use to make important decisions. They are also governed properly and comply with laws of the jurisdictions hosting them. The Best Investment Approaches The next thing after answering the question “ what is an ESG fund?” is to identify the best investment approaches. Because ESG and ETF funds for investing can take different forms, from equities to bonds, there is no one-fits-all approach. So, here are some of the best approaches to consider: Restriction screening : ESG funds often opt out of organizations that are known to go against sustainability goals. So, you might want to check the fund with such screening for assurance against involvement in things like tobacco, firearms, and child labour. ESG integration : This is a hybrid approach employed for financial analysis to assess bonds and equities . This approach encourages investors to strike a 50/50 balance in the focus on financial and sustainability outlook . The good thing about ESG is that the concept has become an important part of organization management, with most companies releasing regular ESG audits for review by investors. Thematic engagement : This refers to an organization’s involvement in sectors that are dedicated to matters of ESG issues. Shareholder engagement : Involving shareholders directly can help to advance ESG investing. More companies are now roping them in to help craft ESG initiatives as a way of earning their trust and boosting revenue. Tips for Selecting the Best ESG Funds How do you identify the right ESG funds to invest in? It is important to have a good strategy for it, and the following four tips can help you narrow down to the best funds for better financial, environmental and social results. Set Out Clear Goals The first step is determining what you plan to achieve through ESG investing . Then, formalize them as the targeted investing goals. This can be very useful in defining the ESG investing strategy. Develop a Clear Plan to Achieve the Objectives Now, establish the amount of money that you want to use and the ESG factors of interest. Then, craft a plan to identify the environmental, social and governance (ESG) funds with assets that can align the capital at hand and companies that share your values. Therefore, it might be crucial to rethink what your priorities and targeted impact are. For example, what do you target with the etf funds? Should you focus on cutting down greenhouse gasses (GHG) as a method of addressing global warming or promoting biodiversity restoration? Diversify Your Investment As an investor, one of the rules of thumb is that you should never put all eggs in one basket. Therefore, you should look for the ESG mutual funds that spread funds as a method of risk management. If the fund has been in operation for some time, consider reviewing its recent performance. The insights can help to provide a clear idea of possible future sustainable performance of the selected companies in the months and years to come. Analyze Different Resources At this point, it is time to dive deeper into the selected ESG fund and the companies that support it. Here, you need to do a thorough analysis and identify the risks/ rewards of the fund. To avoid being biased, consider using multiple resources that provide info about the companies involved. Here are some of the main questions that you need to ask: What are the fees that should be paid for the fund? How do they compare to other funds? What specific criterion is employed by the fund when defining the portfolio holding? What areas do you desire the funds to be invested in? How does the fund discuss the ESG practices ? Talk to an Expert for Help Even with the tips we have listed above, many are those who find identifying the right ESG fund challenging. In such a situation, consider working with an expert for assistance to identify the right funds. Professionals can help you to understand how ESG funds work and the best funds to target. At Diginex.com , we have ESG experts waiting to hold your hand and ensure the preset investment objectives are achieved. Talk to us today for all the assistance you want concerning ESG funds. ‍ ‍

title: 6 signs your firm has outgrown Airtable as its source of truth
summary: Airtable rarely fails all at once. Here are 6 concrete signs your firm's operations have outgrown it and what to do.
body_text: Nobody wakes up one day and decides their Airtable setup needs to change. It's usually a slower thing. A base that used to feel tidy now has three "temporary" duplicate views nobody remembers creating. An automation stopped running after the workspace reached its monthly limit. Someone on the team is still copying numbers into a spreadsheet every Friday because two systems don't quite line up. None of that is a single breaking point. It's six or seven small signs stacking up, and by the time they're obvious, the firm has usually been living with the workaround for months without naming it. TL;DR Airtable's record limits scale from 1,000 on Free to 500,000+ on Enterprise Scale, but most firms don't hit the record ceiling first, they start running into operational limits: permissions, automations, and per-editor costs ( Airtable, 2026 ). Six concrete signs to check for: duplicated interfaces per client, climbing per-editor costs, automations quietly failing, permission workarounds, manual reconciliation between tools, and a growing list of "we'll fix that later" data fixes. Outgrowing Airtable doesn't have to mean leaving it. For many firms, the fix is keeping Airtable as the data layer and consolidating the operational layer, permissions, workflows, client access, on top of it. The right next step depends on how many of these signs you're seeing, not just one in isolation. What does it actually mean to outgrow Airtable? Outgrowing Airtable isn't about running out of storage. Airtable's record limits are generous enough that most professional services firms never hit them (see the table below). What actually happens is quieter: the base still holds the data fine, but the systems built around it, permissions, automations, client access, billing, start requiring more manual work than the team would like. Plan Records per base Automation runs / month Starting price Free 1,000 100 $0 Team 50,000 25,000 $20/editor/mo (annual) Business 125,000 100,000 $45/editor/mo (annual) Enterprise Scale 500,000+ 500,000 Custom For the full picture of what each plan includes and what triggers an upgrade, see our 2026 Airtable pricing breakdown . What are the 6 signs your firm has outgrown Airtable? 1. You're duplicating the same interface or view for every client Airtable Interfaces cap out at 50 per base. Long before firms hit that number, they've usually already built the habit of copying an interface, tweaking a filter, and calling it done for the next client. Each copy needs its own edits when the underlying process changes. If updating one field means updating it in fifteen places, that's usually a sign the setup could benefit from a different approach. We cover the mechanics of this specific cap in the Airtable automation limit nobody warns you about , which is often the sibling problem to interface duplication. 2. Your per-editor costs are climbing faster than your headcount Airtable bills per editor, and "editor" is defined broadly: a contractor who edits weekly, a finance reviewer who comments occasionally, a freelancer brought on for one engagement. All of them count as a full paid seat. Firms routinely discover, six months in, that they're paying for editors who log in once a month. That gradual cost increase if often one of the clearest signs the pricing model no longer matches how the team actually works. 3. You're spending more time checking whether automations are running Airtable's automation runs are capped by plan, and when the cap hits, automations pause until the limit resets or the workspace is upgraded, with no in-app warning next to the automation itself. Client onboarding sequences, invoice reminders, and status notifications can be missed until someone notices a workflow didn't happen as expected. If this sounds familiar, it's worth checking your current automation usage before it becomes an issue. 4. You're building workarounds instead of real permissions Airtable's sharing model was primarily designed for internal collaboration, not for showing 40 different clients 40 different slices of the same base. The common workaround, filtered views tied to a user's email, works up to a point, then breaks down as soon as you need field-level control (showing one client their project status but hiding your internal margin notes, for example). When the permission model requires this much manual scaffolding, the base is starting to stretch beyond its original strengths. 5. Someone is manually reconciling data between Airtable and 2 or 3 other tools This is the sign that costs the most time and shows up the least on any dashboard. A project management tool, an invoicing tool, and Airtable, each holding a piece of the same client record, not always perfectly in sync. According to Asana's Anatomy of Work Index (2026) , roughly 60% of the average workday already goes to work about work, communicating about tasks, hunting down information, and switching between apps, rather than the work itself. Manual reconciliation between tools is exactly the kind of task that index is describing, and it tends to fall on whoever is most conscientious on the team, often without anyone really noticing how much time it adds up to. 6. Your "we'll fix that later" list of data fixes keeps growing, not shrinking Every base accumulates a few of these: a field that should be a linked record but isn't, a status option that got renamed everywhere except in three old views, a duplicate table nobody's brave enough to delete. One or two of these is normal maintenance debt. A growing list that nobody has time to touch is a sign the base has more operational complexity than the team has bandwidth to manage inside Airtable's native tools alone. How many of these signs actually mean it's time to act? One sign on its own usually just means a cleanup task. Two or three, especially numbers 2, 3, and 5 together, usually mean the operational layer around Airtable is starting to outgrow what filtered views and native automations can carry, even if the data itself still fits comfortably inside the record limit. This is where it's worth being precise about what "outgrowing Airtable" actually requires. It doesn't require leaving Airtable. FD Works , for example, kept Airtable as their base and added a dedicated frontend on top specifically to improve the client-facing side of this equation. As Jonathan G, their team lead, put it: "Noloco enabled us to put a very professional frontend on top of our Airtable base." Redrock Entertainment shows the cost side of the same pattern. Their team had hit signs 1 and 2 directly: duplicated Airtable interfaces across more than 100 seats had, in their own words, "become a nightmare to manage," and every lightweight edit still required a full-priced editor seat. Redrock kept Airtable as the source of truth and added Noloco as the operating layer on top. "We've probably cut our annual software cost by about 60%," says Jesse VanDenKooy, Technology Solutions Architect at Redrock Entertainment. Same underlying move as FD Works, consolidating the operational layer rather than the data, just measured in the cost signs instead of the client-facing ones. What are the options once you've outgrown Airtable's operational layer? There are genuinely three paths, not two, and the right one depends on how much of the six signs above apply. Approach Best fit if Noloco Stay on Airtable alone Fewer than 2 of the 6 signs apply, and use is purely internal Not needed yet Keep Airtable as the data layer, add a frontend Signs 1, 3, or 4 apply: client access, permissions, or automations are the bottleneck, not the data itself Noloco connects directly to Airtable , adding branded portals, field-level permissions, and a dedicated workflow engine while your base stays exactly where it is Consolidate onto one operating system Signs 2, 5, and 6 apply: costs, reconciliation, and structural debt are all compounding across multiple tools Noloco can also serve as the primary database, retiring Airtable entirely or keeping it for a narrow, specific use case. See Noloco vs Airtable for a full side-by-side Firms rarely need to decide this in one leap. Most start in the middle row and only rethink their setup further once the reconciliation and cost signs (2, 5, 6) start outweighing the convenience of keeping Airtable as the single source of truth. For a broader look at what that consolidated setup looks like in practice, see consultancy management software: best tools in 2026 . Final thoughts Most teams don't outgrow Airtable overnight. It's usually a series of small operational signals that become more noticeable as the business grows. It's six small signs, duplicated interfaces, creeping seat costs, quiet automation failures, permission workarounds, manual reconciliation, and a growing backlog of data fixes, each one tolerable on its own, worth paying attention to together. The point isn't to panic at the first sign. It's to actually count how many apply, because that number, more than any single feature gap, is what tells you whether you need a cleanup afternoon or a real conversation about whether it's time to rethink the operational layer around your Airtable data. Frequently asked questions How many records can a single Airtable base hold? It depends on the plan: 1,000 on Free, 50,000 on Team, 125,000 on Business, and 500,000+ on Enterprise Scale ( Airtable, 2026 ). Most professional services firms hit operational limits, like automation runs or per-editor costs, before they hit the record ceiling. What's the difference between outgrowing Airtable and just needing more seats? Needing more seats is a straightforward upgrade. Outgrowing Airtable means the operational layer around it, permissions, automations, client access, requires ongoing manual workarounds that a plan upgrade doesn't fix. Do you have to migrate everything at once, or can Airtable stay for part of the operation? No single-cutover requirement exists. Many firms keep Airtable as the data layer and add a dedicated frontend on top first, only consolidating fully onto one system later if cost, reconciliation, or structural signs keep compounding. Is per-editor pricing the main reason firms move off Airtable? It's one of the most common reasons, particularly for firms with many occasional contributors, but it's rarely the only reason. It usually combines with automation limits, permission gaps, or reconciliation overhead. What's the actual first step in addressing these signs? Count how many of the six signs genuinely apply to your firm right now. One or two usually means a targeted fix. Three or more, especially cost, reconciliation, and automation failures together, usually means it's worth evaluating a dedicated operational layer. Does consolidating onto one system always mean giving up Airtable entirely? No. Some firms retire Airtable completely, others keep it for a narrow, specific use case (like a shared internal reference table) while others keep Airtable as the data layer and introduce a dedicated operational layer for workflows, permissions and client collaboration. title: The Lamborghini Portofino Concept Paved the Way for Chrysler’s Cab-Forward Aspirations
summary: The Chrysler LH platform was a major turning point for the automaker, an early ’90s coming-out party that proved it could build more than just K-car–derived econoboxes and minivans. The LH underpinned swoopy sedans like the Dodge Intrepid, Eagle Vision, and the upmarket Chrysler LHS, and the curvy charms of these family cars not only […]
body_text: The Chrysler LH platform was a major turning point for the automaker, an early ’90s coming-out party that proved it could build more than just K-car–derived econoboxes and minivans. The LH underpinned swoopy sedans like the Dodge Intrepid, Eagle Vision, and the upmarket Chrysler LHS, and the curvy charms of these family cars not only unlocked major sales success for the Pentastar as it left the financially shaky 1980s behind, they also sat well in showrooms beside equally striking models like the Dodge Viper roadster and the Dodge Ram pickup. (L-R) Chrysler Concorde, Dodge Intrepid, Eagle Vision Stellantis [ Editor’s note: After you’ve learned about the Portofino, check out Alex Kwanten’s deep dive on the LH platform . ] The design language expressed by these LH cars happens to have an unexpectedly exotic origin story. In fact, while the much-touted “cab forward” look found in Chrysler’s family of four-doors was born in the company’s Pacifica Design Center in San Diego, it had to make a detour to visit an Italian cousin on its passage into production. To untangle the web of the cab-forward design’s ancestry, we sat down with longtime Chrysler design chief Tom Gale, who played a pivotal role in shepherding the LH’s look from early-’80s clay model to global Lamborghini concept to ’90s mainstream sales success. Tom Gale Schicke/ullstein bild/Getty Images Out with the K, in with the Future “I just wanted to prove we weren’t brain-dead as far as design goes,” says Gale, referring to his approach when he took over the role of head of design at Chrysler in April 1985. At the time, the company had just emerged from fulfilling its loan repayment obligations, after the federal government had bailed it out of bankruptcy at the end of the previous decade—a financial reorganization that Chrysler had completed ahead of schedule largely thanks to the popularity of its cheap and cheerful K-platform commuter cars. Despite their popularity, it was clear the K-car party couldn’t go on forever, as there were definite limits to the looks and capabilities offered by these models. President Ronald Reagan and Lee Iacocca discuss the K-car platform. Bettmann Archive/Getty Images “What we were looking at was, what is the future of sedans?” Gale says. “Because the shape [of the K platform] was all too familiar. It came from a philosophy that was more comfortable with vinyl roofs and wire caps and white walls than the stuff of the future. The cars all had these long front-wheel-drive overhangs. We were really trying to figure out what is the most remarkable and effective way to package [a sedan]. And [we] were really trying to push the envelope.” Two designers—Kevin Verduyn and studio boss Tom Tremont—were spearheading the effort at Pacifica, where, Gale says, numerous design studies were underway to try to answer these questions. One pair stood out: the Mojave and the Navajo. The latter caught Gale’s eye at a design review in 1986, and the clay model was brought to the company’s studios at Highland Park, where Verduyn and others continued to refine its look. “Kevin was just phenomenal. A great designer, a futurist, and a wonderful guy,” says Gale. It’s the future-focused nature of the Navajo that intrigued the design chief and proved it had potential to break Chrysler into a post-K-car future. Highland Park, by Way of Italy Lamborghini Portofino concept Stellantis It’s here that the cab-forward path skips across an ocean to engage in a little palace intrigue. In 1987, Chrysler purchased Lamborghini, a company that had spent much of the previous 10 years bouncing from one steward to another . It wasn’t clear exactly why the American automaker was so keen to add the beleaguered supercar builder to its portfolio, but the presence of Lamborghini under the same corporate banner offered an unexpected opportunity for Gale in terms of advancing the work that had been done so far on the Navajo. That chance came from Chrysler executive vice president Bob Lutz. “We had just bought Lamborghini … and we needed something to stir stuff up. And, of course, Bob was always a champion of stirring stuff up,” says Gale. Seeing the Navajo’s potential, Lutz threw his support behind building a full concept version, now renamed the Portofino, by way of the company’s international operations—specifically, Lamborghini. This allowed Gale to avoid significant amounts of budgetary and planning red tape back home. “Lamborghini really had nothing to do with the Portofino,” says Gale. “They were supplying the name and the conduit. It was a way of really attracting attention to something.” Lutz was able to ensure, too, that Chrysler’s design team retained control over the final version of the Portofino concept, something that was a sticking point with Lamborghini from day one. Stellantis “Lamborghini at the time, they were primarily using their designer there, the former Bertone guy, [Marcello] Gandini . He called the Portofino a potato, you know, because basically, if it wasn’t done by him, he didn’t like it. He wasn’t very tactful at all, and he was hard to deal with.” Interacting with Gandini’s team was so difficult that shortly after the Portofino concept was built, Gale clashed with him over the design for the Countach replacement. Finding the Italian completely closed off to any suggestions from Chrysler, Gale ended up taking the Diablo back to Highland Park, completing the design, and then sending not just the completed blueprints but the full tooling model for the surface of the Diablo to Lamborghini. “I know that Lamborghini, being tight with Gandini, they would change it [otherwise]. I was content with being silent about it … and that never came out until the last few years, because nobody wanted to hear about Chrysler designing the Lamborghini,” says Gale. “I knew this was always going to be an argument, so I saved a photo book of the proposals that came about that were done in Highland Park.” Portofino’s Success Births a Cab-Forward Future AutoWeek/Crain Communications The Lamborghini Portofino concept debuted at the Frankfurt Motor Show in 1987, and it made considerable waves. It was built on the same bones as the Jalpa sports coupe and featured a high-revving V-8 engine, but looking back on it today, its influence on LH styling is crystal clear. Swap out the scissor doors and move the engine from the middle to the front of the sedan, and you’ve got a ringer for the original Dodge Intrepid. Dodge Intrepid model transparency Stellantis “Cab forward wasn’t just two words and a term. It was something you could see because it moved the A-pillar forward, it allowed the rear door to expand, and it allowed entry and exit to the car in a much different way,” says Gale. “From a packaging point of view, it became something real. It wasn’t just an advertising term.” Gale points out that the Portofino was “cab-forward on steroids,” primarily because it was a mid-engine car with short overhang at each end. And yet, despite its dramatic layout, much of the concept transferred into production, with even the Portofino’s greenish gold color and wheel design finding its way onto the Intrepid’s order sheet. Stellantis Dodge Intrepid ES Stellantis The Portofino endured long past the time when most concepts are put out to pasture, thanks to policy changes Gale made where concepts returned to the mothership at the end of their show career (rather than being dispersed to dealerships, collectors, or scrap heaps). An unfortunate fire during transport in 1991 nearly destroyed it completely, but instead of walking away from this important piece of its history, Chrysler used its insurance settlement to have California’s Metalcrafters rebuild it to an even higher spec—using real glass rather than the original Plexiglas for the greenhouse, for example. The vehicle remains in the company’s possession today. A Lasting Influence Stellantis Stellantis Lamborghini’s time under the Chrysler umbrella was brief, but there’s no question that using the supercar brand to birth the Portofino concept into the world paid massive dividends for the company’s more mainstream offerings, even if the bull badge was entirely superficial to the vehicle’s development. That wasn’t the only long-lasting gift that the Lamborghini concept bequeathed to the Pentastar, however. “The car was kind of a hit,” says Gale. “I really think it brought a lot of attention to Chrysler that was unexpected. And so (Chrysler CEO) [Lee] Iacocca asked the question, ‘If you can do concept cars like that, why can’t you do production cars?’ And I said, ‘Lee, we’ve been waiting for you to ask that question.’” View this post on Instagram A post shared by Chris Ashworth (@dtrockstar1) With Iacocca’s support, Gale was able to start a production design committee that tied in key executive management—manufacturing, planning, engineering, marketing—into the design process. Suddenly, the design department was on equal footing with the rest of the company’s approach to future planning, giving it a much stronger voice in how Chrysler brought cars to the market. How much of an impact did this have on the automaker’s fortunes? Take a look at the Chrysler of the 1980s and then contrast that against the much rowdier, risk-taking, and eye-catching efforts that emerged in the 1990s. Yes, the Lamborghini Portofino had a direct hand in the success of the LH cars—but its prominence on the international circuit also brought changes that introduced dynamic shapes like the Dodge Neon, the previously mentioned Ram and Viper, the Jeep Grand Cherokee, and the Plymouth Prowler and PT Cruiser, making the decade that followed perhaps the strongest in the company’s history. Tom Gale shows off concept cars at the North American International Auto Show, circa 2000. Clockwise from left: Dodge Viper GTS/R, Jeep Varsity, Dodge MAXXcab, and Chrysler 300 HEMI C. Jeff Kowalsky/AFP/Getty Images The post The Lamborghini Portofino Concept Paved the Way for Chrysler’s Cab-Forward Aspirations appeared first on Hagerty Media .

title: Behind the Bottle: Growing Through Service — Tiara Coleman’s 21 Year Journey at Coca-Cola Consolidated
summary: Tiara Coleman’s 21-year journey at Coca-Cola Consolidated showcases how curiosity, continuous learning, and a passion for serving others can build a meaningful career while inspiring growth, leadership, and community impact.
body_text: For more than two decades, Tiara Coleman has built a career defined by inquisitiveness, service and a profound commitment to helping others achieve their goals. Today, as a raw material specialist on the Product Supply Team in Charlotte, NC, she plays an essential role in assuring Coca-Cola Consolidated’s production operations run seamlessly, coordinating raw material supply, monitoring inventory levels, partnering with vendors, and resolving issues before they impact Teammates or customers. That expertise wasn’t built overnight. Tiara’s journey has taken her through several areas of the business, each experience preparing her for the role she holds today. From Intern to Leader Tiara’s journey with Coca-Cola Consolidated began 21 years ago, when she joined the original call center at the Corporate office in Charlotte as an intern. Her first assignment was calling customers about route changes, something she admits she did not fully grasp at the time. However, over time, as she continued making the calls and learning more about route changes, it led to her being offered a full-time role on the final day of her internship. That moment propelled a career filled with growth, changes and new opportunities. As the Company grew, Tiara transitioned with the call center to a new standalone location where it took on a new name: the Customer Connection Hub. There, she learned to support new customer types and new technologies. “Working with new processes allowed me to meet new Teammates and learn more about the business,” said Tiara. Working closely with Teammates dedicated to Amazon, alternative routes to market and Freestyle drink machines, she built strong relationships and developed skills that would open doors to future roles. Tiara’s next step was joining the Master Data Management (MDM) team, returning to the Corporate office and spending five years learning from peers who helped shape her development. Following that, Tiara took her interchangeable skills to the Product Supply Team as a Product Network Analyst. After another five‑year chapter with the Product Supply Team, she deepened her understanding of the business, and it sparked her interest in raw materials. Today, she incorporates all those experiences in her role as a raw material specialist, where she supports the Company’s mission by ensuring the right materials arrive at the right time and comply with the highest quality standards. Developing a Leadership Mindset Last year, Tiara completed Coke Consolidated’s Aspiring Leadership Course, an experience that reshaped her perspective on leadership. “One of the biggest lessons I learned was that leadership is not defined by a title,” she shared. “You can lead by example, support your peers, and help your team succeed by building trust and understanding.” The program strengthened her communication skills, helped her listen more purposefully and taught her how small actions can positively influence team performance. Since the completion of the course, Tiara has become more intentional about mentoring others, facing challenges directly and promoting a collaborative, supportive workplace. Finding Fulfillment in Growth When asked what she enjoys most about working at Coca-Cola Consolidated, Tiara points to the Company’s commitment to growth, innovation, and relationships. “It’s an environment where you can grow professionally while still feeling connected to the people you work with,” she said. She finds inspiration in seeing her Teammates rise quickly through the organization’s ranks and by the several professional development tools and programs the Company provides, such as Percipio and Foundations of Leadership, which benefit Teammates and their growth. “It’s inspiring to see how Coke Consolidated intentionally invests in its Teammates.” And she feels empowered every day. Whether it’s a Teammate reaching out because someone recommended her, or she’s invited to speak to a department about her role, those moments remind her of the impact she has. An Environment That Continues To Evolve Tiara has witnessed the Company’s culture evolve significantly since she joined in 2005. Throughout her career, she has had the opportunity to collaborate with new teams, learn from colleagues and navigate through different career paths. A vital moment came when mentors motivated her to shadow other departments and attend the Product Supply Experience. That experience helped her discern she wanted to help other Teammates grow. She wanted to serve through coaching, mentoring, teaching and supporting operations. “Being able to serve your peers opens so many opportunities to teach, learn, coach and network,” she said. “It has been awesome and a great development for my career.” Serving the Community and Living the Purpose Volunteering is another one of Tiara’s favorite parts of being a Coke Consolidated Teammate. She sees service as a humbling and grounding experience. “It’s a reminder that everyone has not walked the same life, and you should extend grace to your Teammates and the community we serve.” She hopes that every interaction, whether with a Teammate or a community member, leaves a positive impression and reflects the heart of Coke Consolidated. When asked what she would say to someone considering a career at Coke Consolidated, Tiara doesn’t hesitate: “Apply and join the family. You will not regret your decision. We are excited and ready to welcome you.” To learn more about how you can be a part of Coca-Cola Consolidated, visit Work4Coke.com Share this story! title: Praxis Precision Medicines, Inc. Announces Inducement Grants Under Nasdaq Listing Rule 5635(c)(4)
summary: BOSTON, July 02, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Praxis Precision Medicines, Inc. (Nasdaq: PRAX), a fully integrated, leading central nervous system (CNS)...
body_text: BOSTON, July 02, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Praxis Precision Medicines, Inc. (Nasdaq: PRAX), a fully integrated, leading central nervous system (CNS) precision neuroscience biopharmaceutical company, today announced that on July 1, 2026, the Compensation Committee of Praxis’ Board of Directors granted restricted stock unit awards covering an aggregate of 951 shares of its common stock to five new non-executive employees under the Praxis Precision Medicines, Inc. 2024 Inducement Plan (the 2024 Inducement Plan). The restricted stock unit awards were granted as inducements material to the employees’ entering into employment with Praxis in accordance with Nasdaq Listing Rule 5635(c)(4). The 2024 Inducement Plan is used exclusively for the grant of equity awards to individuals who were not previously employees of Praxis, or following a bona fide period of non-employment, as an inducement material to such individuals’ entering into employment with Praxis, pursuant to Nasdaq Listing Rule 5635(c)(4). The restricted stock units will vest in four equal annual installments, subject to the employee’s continued employment with Praxis on each vesting date. About Praxis Praxis Precision Medicines is a fully integrated, leading CNS precision neuroscience biopharmaceutical company, translating insights from genetic epilepsies into the development of therapies for CNS disorders characterized by neuronal excitation-inhibition imbalance. Praxis is applying genetic insights to the discovery and development of therapies for rare and more prevalent neurological disorders through our proprietary small molecule platform, Cerebrum™, and antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) platform, Solidus™, using our understanding of shared biological targets and circuits in the brain. Praxis has established a diversified, multimodal CNS portfolio including multiple programs across movement disorders and epilepsy, with four late-stage product candidates. For more information, please visit www.praxismedicines.com and follow us on Facebook , LinkedIn and Twitter/X .

title: Pyka Unveils Pelican 2: The World’s Largest Autonomous Crop Protection Aircraft
summary: Pyka Unveils Pelican 2: The World’s Largest Autonomous Crop Protection Aircraft
body_text: Pyka Unveils Pelican 2: The World’s Largest Autonomous Crop Protection Aircraft Secures New FAA Authorization for Commercial Operation of Largest Ever UAS and Takes Order for 20 Aircraft in Brazil ‍ ALAMEDA, Calif. (Feb 10, 2025) — Pyka, a leader in autonomous electric aviation, has unveiled its next-generation agricultural spray aircraft, Pelican 2. Featuring an expanded 300-liter payload and a work rate of up to 90 hectares per hour, Pelican 2 is the world’s largest and most productive autonomous electric agricultural aircraft. Pyka has secured FAA authorization for commercial operation of Pelican 2 in the United States, making this the second time Pyka has gained a groundbreaking commercial approval for its uncrewed aerial system (UAS) products. Pelican 2 is the largest UAS ever approved for commercial use by the FAA, followed only by the original Pelican. This milestone reinforces Pyka’s leadership in heavy lift commercial UAS in the U.S. and globally. In addition to its new product line, Pyka has secured a landmark order for 20 aircraft in Brazil, further solidifying its presence in one of the world's largest agricultural markets. This expansion will enable large-scale autonomous aerial application operations in Brazil, boosting efficiency and delivering unprecedented cost savings for the nation’s growers. Since launching its first commercial autonomous spray aircraft in 2021, Pyka has continuously refined its technology to meet the demands of the world’s most challenging agricultural environments. The next-generation Pelican sets a new benchmark for efficiency and performance in aerial application with: Upgraded four-motor electric propulsion system for increased reliability and power Expanded 300-liter payload capacity for longer spray missions and fewer refills Wider 18-meter swath width, supporting multiple spray boom configurations, including hydraulic nozzles and proprietary electric rotary atomizers Dynamic droplet size adjustment to optimize chemical use and minimize drift Five hot-swappable lithium-ion battery sets, ensuring continuous 24/7 operation Advanced LIDAR and RADAR systems for fully autonomous day-and-night spraying, increasing efficacy and extending spray time. With FAA approval secured, the next-generation Pelican is available to purchase from Pyka at a starting price of USD 550,000. “We couldn't be more excited to release Pelican 2,” said Michael Norcia, Co-Founder and Chief Executive Officer at Pyka. “With nearly 5 years of commercial operation under our belt, this aircraft exhibits the reliability, performance, and ease of operation that growers demand. I have no doubt that the features and operating economics of this aircraft will revolutionize aerial application, delivering meaningful cost-savings and spray results for growers.” “Our customers have been instrumental in shaping this product,” said Volker Fabian, Chief Commercial Officer at Pyka. “Through extensive real-world operations, we’ve perfected Pelican’s performance to exceed growers’ expectations. Spray quality, reliability, and seamless operation are at the core of this aircraft, and no other system on the market comes close.” Expanding Global Reach Pyka’s aircraft has already demonstrated its capabilities on a global scale. In 2023, Pyka launched successful commercial operations with Dole in Honduras, deploying Pelican to enhance efficiency and precision in banana crop protection. Building on this momentum, Pyka secured a landmark commercial agreement in July 2024 with SLC Agrícola, one of Brazil's largest agricultural producers, to deliver Pelican for large-scale agricultural use. Shortly after, following its first FAA authorization for commercial operation in the United States, Pyka delivered its aircraft to Heinen Brothers Agra Services, one of North America’s largest aerial application providers. With global food demand rising, Pyka is poised to transform autonomous aerial application, delivering unprecedented efficiency, cost savings, and sustainability to farmers worldwide. Public Debut at World Ag Expo Pelican 2 will make its public debut at the World Ag Expo in Tulare, California, from February 11-13, 2025. It has been recognized as a winner of the 2025 Top-10 New Products Award by the International Agri-Center. About Pyka Pyka is defining the future of safe, environmentally friendly, and cost-effective aviation with autonomous electric airplanes for crop protection and cargo transport. The company's proprietary technology includes autonomous flight control software, flight computers, high energy density batteries, advanced electric propulsion systems, and carbon composite airframes. For more information, visit www.flypyka.com . ‍

title: Why design matters for a web framework: a 7-year evolution
summary: Wasp is a full-stack web framework. After five years of treating design as second-tier, we rebranded it as a technical spec: blueprints, monospace, three colors. Here's why design ended up mattering more for us than for our users.
body_text: Wasp is a full-stack web framework for React and Node.js (imagine Rails for TypeScript, but with frontend included and wired up out-of-the-box), and we've been building it for a little over five years (as a full-time thing). For almost all of that time, we saw design and "branding" as something we shouldn't spend too much time on. A framework is mostly code, we thought: you drive it from a CLI and your editor, there is little visual to look at, and these days an agent reads the docs for you half the time anyway. The most loved frameworks kind of prove the point, with Django and Rails famous and famously plain. Turns out we were wrong, though not in the way you'd expect. What made design start to matter wasn't users or growth - it was us, the people building Wasp and the community around it. This is the story of how we figured that out, and of the rebrand it led to, which shipped as part of Launch Week #12 - the same week Wasp went fully TypeScript-native . Five years of not having a design ​ Same product, five years apart. Very different vibes. Wasp has always had a logo, colors and fonts (ok, the fonts were whatever shipped with Docusaurus). So when I say we didn't have a design, I mean we never sat down to think about it as a whole. There was no central story, no backbone holding everything together, just a bunch of pages that happened to be ours. Here's how it typically went down: with every big release (v0, Alpha, Beta), I'd sit down and convince Martin (my twin brother and co-founder) to let me "rebrand" Wasp. And every single time, I'd do almost the exact same thing: look around for some inspiration (thanks, Supabase), then patch, okay, steal , a few sections together into something that looked decent enough, and ship it. And early on, that was the right call. When you're still proving the product deserves to exist, obsessing over a design system is a great way to burn weeks you don't really have. Plenty of founders do the opposite. They polish pixels on something nobody wants yet (and we witnessed that many times) and we were determined not to be them. But design debt compounds, just like code debt does. Over five years, Wasp itself grew up a lot , and it grew much faster than its design did, until at some point it just overgrew it. The framework got serious, but the brand stayed improvised. You can kind of watch it happen across our old landing pages: stic (before it was called wasp), 2019 01 / 04 And once our design felt broken, there was little motivation to keep it right, so it just kept getting worse. At one point we needed to show a roadmap on the site, so Martin just screenshotted our GitHub project board and pasted it straight in. Low-res, rounded corners not quite matching, with some random background bleeding out around the edges. It stayed up like that for an embarrassingly long time: Our roadmap section. Yes, that is just a screenshot of our GitHub project. Not even properly cropped. Or take the "How does it work?" section right below it. The diagram was originally drawn as a transparent SVG, which broke once the site got a dark mode, so someone slapped a white background behind it to "fix" it. Now it looked fine on the dark version, and noticeably worse everywhere else. Add the orange highlight pills next to the copy, styled in a completely different visual language than anything else on the page, and the whole thing kind of looked like three different sites stitched together: Our old "How it works" section, broken in a few different ways. At some point we just started to feel bad about how unpolished it looked. We couldn't really tell you what users made of it (probably not much), but we could feel it ourselves: Wasp had grown into a serious product that people use for serious things , and it was about time it started looking like one. Looking unpolished made us feel unpolished ​ There was also another reason for finally taking design seriously, harder to pin down, but looking back it's pretty obvious. Looking unpolished slowly does something to you. Every time we shipped a great feature next to a website that looked like a slightly abandoned student project, it sent a quiet little signal we never really meant to send: that maybe we don't actually care all that much. And that signal doesn't only go out to users; it also comes back in. A product that looks like nobody sweated the details slowly starts to feel like one to the people building it, even when, internally, the opposite is completely true. You don't really notice it on any given day, but over five years it compounds. You hesitate a bit before posting the screenshot. You add a caveat before the demo ( "ignore how it looks for a second, just look at what it does" ). You quietly stop wanting to share Wasp with someone whose opinion you actually care about, because they might judge the wrapper instead of the thing inside. And it gets hard to pour your full energy into something you're a tiny bit embarrassed by. So in a real sense, a good part of this rebrand wasn't for users at all. It was for us. We wanted to be able to look at every surface Wasp touches and not flinch, and to feel like the way Wasp looks finally matches how much we actually care about it. Looking back, that's not really vanity but basic hygiene, and we should've done it sooner. The product changed, so the skin had to ​ When we made the call to go all-in on TypeScript , we knew it wasn't a facelift. It changed what Wasp fundamentally is : not a custom language you have to learn, but a framework that meets you where you already are. That forced an uncomfortable question: if someone landed on wasp.sh today, would they actually see that? Honestly, no. The old look still said "quirky side project with a custom language", while the new Wasp is something else: a serious, full-stack TypeScript framework you'd reach for to build a real product. The caterpillar was getting its wings (ok, wasp, but you get the idea), and it couldn't really keep wearing the old skin. So instead of asking ourselves "what looks nice?", we ended up asking a much better question: what is Wasp, actually? Wasp is a spec. So the brand is a blueprint. ​ The core idea behind Wasp has always been the same, DSL or no DSL: you declare what your app is (routes, pages, auth, jobs, the whole skeleton), and Wasp handles all the plumbing under the hood. The high-level spec you define in TypeScript is essentially an engineering drawing of your application, and the framework just builds it. (Quick side note: "Wasp" itself stands for W eb A pplication SP ecification - which is basically how we've always thought about it.) But before we landed there, we explored a lot of other directions. Some internal attempts (mostly me prompting Nano Banana), and we also briefly worked with a few designers who came back with their own takes. AI turned out to be genuinely useful in this phase: you can iterate on entire landing-page mockups in a few minutes and quickly see what does and what doesn't feel like Wasp, and build intuition for what you like. Here's one of mine: One of my early Nano Banana runs. Already leaning hard into the schematic / blueprint angle that ended up shaping the final brand. And here's a small sample of what the designers sent over: (Click to zoom): A few of the directions designers came back with. Honestly, none of them really clicked for us, probably because the process happened too much in isolation from us. After cycling through enough of these, the visual direction we wanted got pretty obvious. Wasp's brand should look like what it is: a technical spec . Blueprints, schematics, annotated diagrams: the kind of stuff engineers draw before they go and build. That single idea ended up driving basically everything in the new identity: The new Wasp brand system. Monospace first. Our primary typeface is JetBrains Mono, backed by IBM Plex Mono. Monospace is the native typography of our world and we just really like how it looks. We were deliberating about using monospace literally everywhere, but in the end decided to settle on titles and subtitles, while the body text in the docs and the blog is IMB Plex Sans - easier on the eyes, but still feels close to the monospace aesthetic. Three colors, and that's it. Wasp Yellow (#F5C842), Ink Black (#111), and a warm paper tone we call Blueprint Paper (#F7F5F0). Yellow and black because, well, wasp. Paper because real engineering drawings live on paper, not on gradients. Sharp corners, visible structure. 90° angles, 2px strokes, no rounded-blob softness anywhere. Our illustrations aren't there to decorate the page. They're schematics: boxes, connectors, annotations, the architecture of your app drawn like a circuit diagram. The mark. The =} symbol, set in a solid square. It's pulled straight from code, works at any size from a favicon to a billboard, and if you squint a bit it still reads as a wasp's wings and antennae. It didn't arrive fully formed, though. The project actually started life as stick (yes, there was a literal photo of a wooden stick), then stic (Specification to Implementation Compiler), and finally wasp . The =} itself only showed up around the Alpha launch in 2020, sitting inside a yellow circle. The 2026 rebrand was basically the moment we finally squared it off and stopped fiddling with it: The Wasp mark, from a stick to a square. Light, on purpose. One thing we very deliberately kept: Wasp stays light theme-first. It would have been the easy, default move to go dark-mode-everything and look like every other devtool out there. But people have always told us that Wasp's look feels happy (warm and approachable in a category that mostly reads as cold and serious), and we didn't want to just throw that away to become another Linear clone. The world already has plenty of near-black landing pages with a purple gradient on top. Blueprint paper is bright, optimistic, and it's ours. Constraints are the whole point - both in design and code ​ Here's the part we honestly didn't expect: the best thing about the new brand isn't really how it looks, but how fast it now makes us move. Two fonts, three colors, one illustration style, and only sharp corners. It sounds restrictive on paper, and it is, but in the best possible way. Before, no one really knew what to reach for, so everyone would just do their own thing each time. Now there's almost nothing to decide. A launch banner, a chart for Twitter, a docs page, a sticker - they all kind of assemble themselves from the same small kit. It's actually the same philosophy as Wasp itself: strong defaults and clear structure don't limit you - they free you up to focus on the parts that actually matter. We even wrote ourselves a proper brandbook in the end, partly because we genuinely needed one, and partly because after five years of winging it, it just felt really, really good to finally have one. The color-system page from our brandbook. We shipped it like a rolling release ​ We didn't flip a switch one morning and unveil a finished new site. We rolled it out the same way we ship software: piece by piece, swapping new parts in while the old ones were still live. So for a while, wasp.sh was a bit of a Frankenstein (honestly, it kind of still is). A shiny new hero sitting on top of an old footer, new buttons next to old cards, fonts not quite agreeing with each other across the page. It looked pretty rough, but the old site already looked rough, so a half-migrated version was still a step up, not a regression. The bar, luckily for us, was very forgiving. And honestly, the awkwardness actually helped. Having a half-finished site sitting out in the open was a little embarrassing, which was kind of the whole point. Nobody really wants a Frankenstein page on the internet with their name on it, so we kept sprinting to fix the next piece before too many people saw it in that state. The embarrassment basically became a deadline we couldn't ignore. And it was the only realistic way we were ever going to get it done. If we'd waited to perfect every pixel and ship it all at once, we'd genuinely still be waiting today. Wasp moves too fast for a big-bang redesign. By the time it was "done", half of it would already be stale. Shipping it in pieces is what actually kept us moving. Designing it changed what we think Wasp is ​ Another thing we found really valuable about this whole process had nothing to do with how anything looked. To draw a thing, you first have to know what the thing actually is . So every design decision kept bouncing back at us as a product question: who is this really for, what do we stand for, what do we actually want to say. Before we knew it, the rebrand had quietly turned into a rewrite. We reworked our words, our positioning, our whole story, and then the new words changed the design, and the new design changed the words again. The two kept reshaping and reinforcing each other. That loop is exactly why we're glad we didn't just hand this whole thing off to someone external. An agency can absolutely make you look good. What it can't really do is the part that turned out to matter most: the way designing the brand forces you to understand, and sometimes redraw, the product itself. That kind of thing only really happens when the people building the product are also the ones drawing it. What do you think? ​ The new look is now live on wasp.sh , across our docs, and everywhere else Wasp shows up. Like everything we ship, it'll keep evolving, and we'd love your honest take: the good, the bad, and the "did it really have to be monospace?". Come tell us on Discord , Twitter/X , or GitHub . 🐝
